q-4771:
First, we need to calculate the velocity function. We can do that by taking the derivative of the position function, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-10t-2) \\  & =2t-10\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m/s}.$ So, we set $v=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2t-10 & =0 \\ 2t & =10 \\ t & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary at $t=5\,\text{s}.$

q-48911:
If the particle moves in the direction of decreasing $x,$ then its velocity is negative.

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{{t}^{2}-4t+6}) \\  & =(2t-4){e}^{{t}^{2}-4t+6}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x$, we must solve $v(t)<0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & <0 \\ (2t-4){e}^{{t}^{2}-4t+6} & <0 \\ 2t-4 & <0 \\ 2t & <4 \\ t & <2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of decreasing $x$ is $[0,2).$

q-73210:
If the particle moves in the direction of increasing $x,$ then its velocity is positive. 

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t{e}^{-2t}) \\  & ={e}^{-2t}(1-2t)\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x$, we solve $v(t)>0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & >0 \\ {e}^{-2t}(1-2t) & >0 \\ 1-2t & >0 \\ 2t & <1 \\ t & <\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of increasing $x$ is $t\in [0,\frac{1}{2}).$

q-7188:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{2}{9}{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}+14t+17) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{t}^{2}+6t+14\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{2}{3}{t}^{2}+6t+14) \\  & =-\frac{4}{3}t+6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-\frac{4}{3}t+6 \\ \frac{4}{3}t & =6 \\ t & =4.5\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t=4.5.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
v(4.5)=-\frac{2}{3}(4.5)^{2}+6(4.5)+14=27.5.
$$

q-109302:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}+3t-2) \\  & =6{t}^{2}-18t+3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{2}-18t+3) \\  & =12t-18\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}12t-18 & =0 \\ t & =\frac{18}{12} \\ t & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the acceleration is zero when $t=\frac{3}{2}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{3}{2}) & =6{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-18(\frac{3}{2})+3 \\  & =6(\frac{9}{4})-27+3 \\  & =\frac{27}{2}-27+3 \\  & =-\frac{21}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

q-49677:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{2x} & ⇒ & v=\frac{{e}^{2x}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{{e}^{2x}}{2}-\int \frac{{e}^{2x}}{2}\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}x{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}(x{e}^{2x}){|}_{0}^{1/2}-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x{e}^{2x}){|}_{0}^{1/2}-\frac{{e}^{2x}}{4}{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2(1/2)}-0\cdot {e}^{2\cdot 0}]-\frac{1}{4}[{e}^{2(1/2)}-{e}^{2\cdot 0}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\frac{e}{2}-0]-\frac{1}{4}[e-1] \\  & =\frac{e}{4}-\frac{e-1}{4} \\  & =\frac{e-e+1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-74087:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 2x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\,\text{d}x & =2x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)}{2}-\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)}{2}\cdot 2\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)\text{d}x & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+8)+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+8)}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-88824:
First, we define the function $f(x)$ as

$$
f(x)=\frac{x-1}{4{x}^{2}+12x+9}.
$$

By factoring its denominator, the function $f(x)$ can be rewritten as

$$
f(x)=\frac{x-1}{(2x+3)^{2}}.
$$

So we're now solving the inequality $f(x)>0.$

The solutions to the equation $f(x)=0$ is $x=1.$  Also, $f(x)$ has a vertical asymptote at $x=-\frac{3}{2}.$ The root and asymptote divide the number line into $3$ subintervals:

$$
(-\infty ,-\frac{3}{2}),\,(-\frac{3}{2},1),\,(1,\infty )
$$

Now, we construct a sign table with the list of the intervals on the top and the list of factors on the left. Filling in the sign table using the usual method, we get the following result:

|  | $(-\infty ,-\frac{3}{2})$ | $(-\frac{3}{2},1)$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x-1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $(2x+3)^{2}$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $f(x)$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |

Finally, to solve the inequality $f(x)>0,$ we look at the bottom row to find out where $f(x)$ is positive.

From the table, we see that $f(x)$ is positive on the interval $(1,\infty ).$

Therefore, we conclude that $f(x)>0$ for all $x\in (1,\infty ).$

q-141314:
Suppose we have a geometric sequence with the first term ${a}_{1}$ and common ratio $r.$ Then, we have the following convergence properties:

- if $|r|<1,$ the sequence is convergent and converges to $0$

- if $|r|>1,$ the sequence is divergent

Moreover, we have the following edge cases:

- if $r=1,$ the sequence is convergent and converges to ${a}_{1}$

- if $r=-1,$ the sequence is divergent

First, we rewrite the sequence in the form ${a}_{n}=a\cdot {r}^{n},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{8\cdot {11}^{n}}{{9}^{n}} \\  & =8\cdot \frac{{11}^{n}}{{9}^{n}} \\  & =8{(\frac{11}{9})}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

We can now see that this is the geometric sequence with $r=\frac{11}{9}.$ 

Since $|r|>1,$ the sequence diverges.

- if $|r|<1,$ the sequence is convergent and converges to $0$

q-141323:
Suppose we have a geometric sequence with the first term ${a}_{1}$ and common ratio $r.$ Then, we have the following convergence properties:

- if $|r|<1,$ the sequence is convergent and converges to $0$

- if $|r|>1,$ the sequence is divergent

Moreover, we have the following edge cases:

- if $r=1,$ the sequence is convergent and converges to ${a}_{1}$

- if $r=-1,$ the sequence is divergent

The given sequence is a geometric sequence with the common ratio $r=\frac{8}{x}.$ 
Since $x$ is positive,  $r$ is also positive, So, the convergence condition is $0<r\le 1.$ 

Therefore, the  sequence converges for 

$$
0<\frac{8}{x}\le 1\,⟹\,x\ge 8.
$$

q-74633:
Suppose we have a geometric sequence with the first term ${a}_{1}$ and common ratio $r.$ Then, we have the following convergence properties:

- if $|r|<1,$ the sequence is convergent and converges to $0$

- if $|r|>1,$ the sequence is divergent

Moreover, we have the following edge cases:

- if $r=1,$ the sequence is convergent and converges to ${a}_{1}$

- if $r=-1,$ the sequence is divergent

First, we rewrite the sequence in the form ${a}_{n}=a\cdot {r}^{n},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{{2}^{n+4}}{{x}^{n}} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{n}\cdot {2}^{4}}{{x}^{n}} \\  & ={2}^{4}\cdot \frac{{2}^{n}}{{x}^{n}} \\  & =16{(\frac{2}{x})}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

 

We see that this is a geometric sequence with the common ratio $r=\frac{2}{x}.$ Since $x$ is positive,  $r$ is also positive. So, the convergence condition is $0<r\le 1.$ 

Therefore, the  sequence converges for 

$$
0<\frac{2}{x}\le 1\,⟹\,x\ge 2.
$$

q-11311:
First, we find $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-y & =0 \\ y(\frac{1}{2}y-1) & =0 \\ y & =0,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14032052/assets/29cf73562152cb8201c8e93545ca7f8416aa8412217cfc9dcdaf87e5b794d971.png)

We want to find the area between the curve $x=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-y$ and the $y$-axis from  $y=0$ to $y=2.$ To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{2}-{\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(2)^{3}}{3}-0)-(\frac{(2)^{2}}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}-2 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis, we obtained a negative number. So the area that we want is $\frac{2}{3}.$
